claims.text: The initial equiatomic FeNiCrMn alloy is single-phase FCC.
The initial FeNiCrMn crystal contains thermal vacancies and potential vacancy clusters.
The initial crystal contains no pre-existing stacking faults or twins.
Shockley partial-dislocation nucleation in FeNiCrMn is thermally activated.
Shockley partial dislocations nucleate preferentially at pre-existing vacancy clusters or stacking-fault embryos.
Vacancy clusters locally reduce stacking-fault energy and thereby lower the critical resolved shear stress for dislocation nucleation.
At low temperature, insufficient thermal vibrations prevent nucleation at perfect-lattice sites and force nucleation at vacancy clusters.
Vacancy-cluster-mediated Shockley partials produce intrinsic stacking faults and HCP-like local structures.
The maximum yield stress is higher for the <110> loading orientation than for the <11-1> orientation.
The <110> orientation increases yield stress by aligning the active slip-plane normal closer to the loading axis and maximizing resolved shear stress, while <11-1> has lower Schmid factors.
The <110>-oriented crystals will have a yield stress 15–20% higher than the <11-1>-oriented crystals.
The HCP-like regions are transient stacking faults rather than a true phase transformation.
The HCP-like regions lack long-range lattice-parameter shifts and have continuous fault boundaries.
The HCP-like regions are bounded by partial dislocations rather than coherent phase interfaces.
Stacking-fault width will scale with applied strain without producing diffraction-peak splitting characteristic of a bulk phase transformation.
Yield strength is typically insensitive to strain rate from 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1.
Yield strength decreases with increasing temperature because thermal activation facilitates dislocation motion.
The cited CoNiCrFeMn nanowire study reports twinning and martensitic transformation at 300 K.
The cited evidence does not explicitly detail vacancy-cluster-mediated nucleation in FeNiCrMn.

contradictions.description: The initial state excludes pre-existing stacking faults, but the nucleation hypothesis invokes pre-existing stacking-fault embryos as preferred sites without explaining how such embryos differ from the excluded faults or when they form.

The orientation argument says <110> maximizes resolved shear stress yet also produces a higher macroscopic yield stress. Under a Schmid-law argument, a larger resolved shear stress per unit applied stress would ordinarily reach the CRSS at a lower applied stress, so the stated mechanism does not coherently imply the predicted ordering.
